description: Down in the basement the practical bench is lined with first-years' boilers, each waiting for a qualified hand to test it before it is lit. The tester has not come down, and the first-years will not leave their boilers. It is gone nine, and nobody has eaten since a bun at noon. A spirit stove sits at the end of the bench beside a dented pot, and six first-years in scorched aprons turn toward you as the only person present who has been seen to cook.

options.label: Make supper from the cupboard's two onions and an unlabelled tin, and hope the pot forgives you.

success.text: It is brown, thick and shapeless, and it is gone in four minutes. Someone scrapes the pot with a No. 4 spanner. Two Rustmoor rations come out of a satchel and are pressed into your hands for the road, with the solemnity usually reserved for pensions.

failure.text: The pot catches, and so does your sleeve. Somebody notes the smell as an example of incomplete combustion. The first-years eat bread and look at you kindly, which is worse.

options.label: Stir two measures of your barley meal into a proper porridge for the bench.

success.text: The porridge is plain and hot and exactly enough. The bench eats in a silence broken only by spoons and, once, a boiler ticking as it cools. Somebody writes your name in the margin of a pressure table.

options.label: Fry two cuts of your salt pork, and accept two rations in the bench's thanks.

success.text: The pork spits across the stove, and the basement smells for an hour of a Sunday dinner. The first-years eat standing, still holding their gauges. Two of them leave a Rustmoor ration each on the pot lid, wrapped in a page of laboratory notes, without a word.
